---
title: "Identifying document language"
subtitle: "Treat language guesses as fallible classifications"
description: "Compare two language detectors on short Riverton samples and learn why no label can be safer than a wrong label."
categories: [documents, language identification, workforce research]
---

Short notes in several languages require routing before content annotation.
The coordinator must assign each note to people who can read its language.

`Open house.` exposes the problem. A person reads the two-word notice as English,
while a language detector may have too little evidence to say.

**Language identification** is a classification problem. A classifier assigns a
label from a fixed set, such as `en` for English or `es` for Spanish. The risk
is either a wrong code or no answer, which leaves the item without a route.
This lesson compares those outcomes for two detectors on a small teaching file.

::: {.callout-note}
The Riverton inbox and the language samples are fictional teaching materials.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you will learn

Use this lesson to practice how to:

- execute two local language detectors on fixed samples.
- compare detector output with recorded labels.
- separate agreement from correctness.
- explain why short texts are hard to classify.
- describe why returning `NA` can be safer than a wrong language code.
:::

```{r}
#| include: false

options(warn = 2)
stopifnot(identical(getOption("warn"), 2L))
```

## Load the labelled samples

The setup records detector versions and measures text length. It executes the local
CLD2 and CLD3 detectors and calculates a file fingerprint. The author wrote
the short samples for teaching.

```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(stringr)
library(cld2)
library(cld3)
library(digest)

language_path <- "data/riverton/language-samples.csv"
language_samples <- read_csv(
  language_path,
  na = character(),
  col_types = cols(
    sample_id = col_character(),
    written_in = col_character(),
    text = col_character()
  )
)

reference_metadata <- read_csv(
  "data/riverton/riverton-reference-metadata.csv",
  na = character(),
  col_types = cols(
    artifact = col_character(),
    description = col_character(),
    source = col_character(),
    license = col_character(),
    created_on = col_character(),
    fingerprint = col_character()
  )
)

language_reference <- reference_metadata |>
  filter(artifact == "language-samples.csv")

sample_fingerprint <- digest::digest(
  paste(read_lines(language_path), collapse = "\n"),
  algo = "sha256",
  serialize = FALSE
)

recorded_fingerprint <- reference_metadata |>
  filter(artifact == "language-samples.csv") |>
  pull(fingerprint)

detector_versions <- tibble(
  detector = c("cld2", "cld3"),
  package_version = c(
    as.character(packageVersion("cld2")),
    as.character(packageVersion("cld3"))
  )
)

display_samples <- language_samples |>
  mutate(
    display_text = str_c(
      "<span lang=\"",
      written_in,
      "\">",
      text,
      "</span>"
    )
  )
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  detector_versions,
  col.names = c("Detector package", "Version"),
  caption = "Detector package versions for this run",
  row.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  tibble(
    file = language_path,
    sha256 = sample_fingerprint
  ),
  col.names = c("File", "SHA-256 fingerprint"),
  caption = "Fingerprint for the author-written language sample file",
  row.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  display_samples |>
    select(sample_id, written_in, display_text),
  col.names = c("Sample", "Recorded language", "Text"),
  caption = "Eight labelled language samples used for detection",
  row.names = FALSE,
  escape = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(language_samples), 8L),
  identical(
    names(language_samples),
    c("sample_id", "written_in", "text")
  ),
  identical(language_samples$text[7], "Open house."),
  identical(nrow(language_reference), 1L),
  identical(sample_fingerprint, recorded_fingerprint),
  identical(
    sample_fingerprint,
    "fa84ffaf608578b8dd0e4f0dbc7425049cd9d362e9d41a1773078973afeccf67"
  ),
  all(str_detect(detector_versions$package_version, "^\\d+\\.\\d+"))
)

stopifnot(
  !any(str_detect(language_samples$text, "[<>&]")),
  all(str_detect(display_samples$display_text, fixed("<span lang=")))
)
```

The `written_in` column records the author's intended language rather than an
independently assessed annotation. The Spanish [Casa abierta.]{lang="es"} is
grammatical. As an event notice, it is a **calque**, a direct translation,
rather than an idiomatic phrase. The results describe the detector versions
printed above. A different package version can return different codes for the
same strings.

## Run two detectors

CLD2 and CLD3 are trained language detectors. `NA` means the detector returned no
language label. The detectors classify the supplied characters rather than
understand the complete situation around a note.

```{r}
detected_samples <- language_samples |>
  mutate(
    characters = str_length(text),
    words = str_count(text, boundary("word")),
    length_group = if_else(characters <= 13L, "short", "long"),
    cld2_language = cld2::detect_language(text),
    cld3_language = cld3::detect_language(text),
    cld2_match = !is.na(cld2_language) & cld2_language == written_in,
    cld3_match = !is.na(cld3_language) & cld3_language == written_in,
    display_text = str_c(
      "<span lang=\"",
      written_in,
      "\">",
      text,
      "</span>"
    )
  )

open_house <- detected_samples |>
  filter(text == "Open house.")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  detected_samples |>
    select(
      sample_id,
      written_in,
      display_text,
      characters,
      words,
      cld2_language,
      cld3_language
    ),
  col.names = c(
    "Sample",
    "Recorded language",
    "Text",
    "Characters",
    "Words",
    "CLD2",
    "CLD3"
  ),
  caption = "Language detector output for each sample",
  row.names = FALSE,
  escape = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(
    detected_samples$cld2_language,
    c("en", "en", "es", "fr", "de", NA, NA, NA)
  ),
  identical(
    detected_samples$cld3_language,
    c("en", "en", "es", "fr", "de", NA, NA, NA)
  ),
  identical(open_house$written_in, "en"),
  is.na(open_house$cld2_language),
  is.na(open_house$cld3_language),
  identical(open_house$characters, 11L),
  identical(open_house$words, 2L)
)
```

Both installed detectors **abstain**, or return no label, on `Open house.`.
The `NA` result lets a person examine the item instead of automatic routing
with an incorrect code.

## Count matches, abstentions, and label differences

Agreement between two detectors does not prove correctness. They can share
training data patterns and make the same mistake. The recorded labels let the
team count what happened on these eight examples.

```{r}
detector_counts <- tibble(
  detector = c("CLD2", "CLD3"),
  matched_recorded_label = c(
    sum(detected_samples$cld2_match),
    sum(detected_samples$cld3_match)
  ),
  no_label = c(
    sum(is.na(detected_samples$cld2_language)),
    sum(is.na(detected_samples$cld3_language))
  )
) |>
  mutate(
    differed_from_recorded_label =
      nrow(detected_samples) - matched_recorded_label - no_label
  )
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  detector_counts,
  col.names = c(
    "Detector",
    "Matched recorded label",
    "No label",
    "Different from recorded label"
  ),
  caption = "Detector outcomes across the eight labelled samples",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(detector_counts$matched_recorded_label, c(5L, 5L)),
  identical(detector_counts$no_label, c(3L, 3L)),
  identical(detector_counts$differed_from_recorded_label, c(0L, 0L)),
  identical(sum(detected_samples$cld2_match), 5L),
  identical(sum(detected_samples$cld3_match), 5L)
)
```

Each detector matches 5 of the 8 recorded labels. It returns no label for
3 of the 8 and an incorrect label for 0 of the 8. Those fractions describe
this small teaching file, not detector accuracy on a workforce archive.

## Compare short and longer text

Text length affects the amount of evidence a detector receives. This file is too
small to give an estimate of the length effect. There is no principled cutoff here. The
13-character line separates the two shortest strings from the other 6 examples.

```{r}
length_summary <- detected_samples |>
  group_by(length_group) |>
  summarise(
    samples = n(),
    cld2_matches = sum(cld2_match),
    cld2_no_label = sum(is.na(cld2_language)),
    cld3_matches = sum(cld3_match),
    cld3_no_label = sum(is.na(cld3_language)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(length_group)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  length_summary,
  col.names = c(
    "Length group",
    "Samples",
    "CLD2 matches",
    "CLD2 no label",
    "CLD3 matches",
    "CLD3 no label"
  ),
  caption = "Detector outcomes by sample length in this file",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(length_summary$length_group, c("long", "short")),
  identical(length_summary$samples, c(6L, 2L)),
  identical(length_summary$cld2_matches, c(5L, 0L)),
  identical(length_summary$cld2_no_label, c(1L, 2L)),
  identical(length_summary$cld3_matches, c(5L, 0L)),
  identical(length_summary$cld3_no_label, c(1L, 2L))
)
```

The two shortest samples produce no matches because both detectors abstain.
Among the six other samples, each detector matches 5 recorded labels and abstains
on 1. The Dutch sentence is long enough to read by eye, but both detectors return
`NA`.

## A wrong code is worse than no code

The eight labelled samples produced no wrong codes, but wrong codes remain
possible. The author selected the next string because it produces an incorrect
code. This one case demonstrates a failure. It does not give an estimate of its rate.
Its length is just above the arbitrary 13-character cutoff.

```{r}
short_probe <- tibble(
  text = c("Open house.", "Evening class."),
  recorded_language = "en"
) |>
  mutate(
    characters = str_length(text),
    cld2_language = cld2::detect_language(text),
    cld3_language = cld3::detect_language(text),
    cld2_match = !is.na(cld2_language) & cld2_language == recorded_language,
    cld3_match = !is.na(cld3_language) & cld3_language == recorded_language
  )
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  short_probe |>
    select(text, recorded_language, cld2_language, cld3_language),
  col.names = c("Text", "Recorded language", "CLD2", "CLD3"),
  caption = "Two short English probes and their detected languages",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(short_probe$characters, c(11L, 14L)),
  all(is.na(short_probe$cld2_language)),
  identical(short_probe$cld3_language, c(NA, "lb")),
  identical(short_probe$cld2_match, c(FALSE, FALSE)),
  identical(short_probe$cld3_match, c(FALSE, FALSE))
)
```

`Evening class.` is English in this teaching probe. CLD2 returns `NA`, while CLD3
returns `lb`, the ISO 639-1 code for Luxembourgish. For routing, the abstention
is safer because a person examines the item before selecting a queue.

These eight samples are all written in the Latin alphabet, so this page shows
nothing about other writing systems. That is a limit of the file, not a
reassurance.

## Language identification in production

`cld2` and `cld3` illustrate the routing problem. Models such as Meta's
`fasttext` are common alternatives for fast language identification. Deployment
requires these considerations:

- **Language scope and BCP 47**: State which languages the project handles. Record languages with standard BCP 47 tags, such as `en-US`, rather than informal names.
- **Per-language recall**: A model's overall accuracy hides its failures. Always measure recall *per language*, because models routinely fail on low-resource languages.
- **Code-switching**: The single-label `cld2::detect_language()` and
  `cld3::detect_language()` calls used here return one document label. Mixed
  language text needs a span-level or token-level detector, or a person to
  examine the text. Code-switching means alternating languages within the text.
  Single-label behavior does not describe every model.
- **Probability vs. certainty**: A confidence score such as `0.95` is not necessarily a calibrated probability. Calibration means predicted probabilities agree with observed frequencies. The internal score alone does not establish that agreement.

## What to remember

- Language identification may return a code or no label.
- Agreement between detectors does not prove that a language code is correct.
- The eight-row file is an inspection exercise: both detectors returned no label
  for the two shortest strings rather than a guess.
- Returning `NA` can be safer than sending text to the wrong language queue.

People must examine items with `NA` results and codes from short text before
routing them. The selected probe demonstrates a possible wrong code. The
eight-row file demonstrates abstention instead of an incorrect assignment.
